column1: What is the Chomsky hierarchy triple equivalence for regular languages?
column2: A language is regular iff it is recognized by a finite automaton, iff it is generated by a regular grammar, iff it is described by a regular expression.

column1: Why can't a finite automaton match balanced constructs (e.g., nested parentheses)?
column2: A DFA/NFA has only bounded memory (a finite number of states) and cannot count without bound or remember arbitrarily long prefixes, which is required to track nesting depth.

column1: What does Kleene's theorem establish about NFAs and DFAs?
column2: Any language accepted by an NFA is also accepted by some DFA, and both describe exactly the same class of languages: the regular languages expressible by regular expressions.

column1: Compare the time and space complexity trade-offs between NFA simulation and DFA matching for a pattern of length m on input of length n.
column2: NFA simulation: O(m) states, O(m·n) match time. DFA: up to 2^m states in the worst case (subset construction), but O(n) match time independent of m once built.

column1: What is the key architectural trade-off that determines whether a regex engine is vulnerable to ReDoS?
column2: Backtracking NFA engines (PCRE, Python re, Java, .NET) support backreferences/lookaround but risk O(2^n) exponential worst-case time; pure NFA engines (RE2, Rust regex, Go regexp) guarantee O(m·n) time but cannot support backreferences.

column1: Why is a pattern like (.+)\1 not a regular language?
column2: Backreferences require remembering an arbitrarily long matched substring and comparing it later, which demands unbounded memory — this makes the language context-free (or beyond), not regular, so no DFA can recognize it.

column1: What distinguishes POSIX leftmost-longest semantics from PCRE leftmost-first semantics? Give the example with (a|ab) against 'ab'.
column2: POSIX returns the longest match among all leftmost matches, so (a|ab) on 'ab' returns 'ab'. PCRE returns the first alternative found via depth-first traversal, so it returns 'a'.

column1: What is the structural pattern that causes catastrophic backtracking, and why?
column2: Patterns of the form (X+)+Y where X and Y can match overlapping/same characters. The engine cannot prune ambiguous paths, so each failure triggers exponential re-exploration of partitioning possibilities for the repeated group.

column1: What is the practical consequence of the fact that most production regex engines (PCRE, Python re, Java, .NET) use backtracking NFA simulation rather than a pure DFA?
column2: They support rich features like capturing groups and backreferences impossible in a pure DFA, but sacrifice the O(n) worst-case guarantee, risking exponential-time blowup on adversarial input.

column1: What does subset construction do when converting an NFA to a DFA, and what is its worst-case cost?
column2: It builds each DFA state as a subset of NFA states that could be simultaneously active, which can result in up to 2^m DFA states for an NFA with m states in the worst case.

column1: Which engines guarantee O(m·n) worst-case matching time by avoiding backtracking entirely, and what feature do they sacrifice?
column2: RE2, Rust's regex crate, and Go's regexp package guarantee O(m·n) time via Thompson NFA simulation, but they sacrifice support for backreferences (and some lookaround constructs).

column1: Who introduced the algorithm of compiling a regex into an NFA and simulating it without backtracking, and in what year?
column2: Ken Thompson, in his 1968 paper 'Programming Techniques: Regular Expression Search Algorithm.'
